title: PTA Three Ways
setting: School pickup, 3:15pm. The same pastime - talking about kids - is running at three different tables by the gate, and it sounds like a different conversation each time.

L1.line: Kids today just don't get taught respect anymore - it's the screens, I'm telling you, every single one of them.
cues: moral judgment, not a specific example
L1.question: Rosita's doing the same pastime every parent at the gate does - talking about kids. Which register is she doing it in?

options.text: Parent - a pre-judged opinion about the world, delivered as settled fact.
options.feedback: Right - sweeping, moral, certain, about "kids today" in general. This is the Parental register of the pastime.

options.text: Adult - she's reporting something she's actually observed and checked.
options.feedback: Adult would be specific and tentative ("my son's screen time went up this term, and..."), not a sweeping verdict about every child.

options.text: Child - she's replaying an old feeling from her own childhood.
options.feedback: Child register of this pastime sounds more like anxious or wistful memory, not a confident moral verdict about the world.

L1.lesson: The same pastime topic - kids and parenting - gets played in different ego-state registers: Parent delivers settled, moral opinions about the world ('kids today...'); Adult trades specific, checkable information; Child replays old feelings. Same words-shaped activity, three different internal processes.

L2.intro: Camellia can match whichever register she's handed, or cross it. Same pastime, three possible levels.

beats.line: Kids today just don't get taught respect anymore - it's the screens, I'm telling you.

options.text: Match her: "Exactly, it's all the screens, my kid's the same."
options.outcome: Rosita nods, satisfied. They've spent two minutes agreeing about screens without checking anything. Comfortable, unremarkable, over by the time the bell rings.
options.lesson: Matching a Parent-register pastime keeps it comfortable and complementary - that's not a failure, pastimes exist partly to sound each other out safely; it's just not the only option.

options.text: Offer something specific and checkable: "Actually my son's teacher said his focus has been fine this term - it was rough in September, but it evened out."
options.outcome: Rosita pauses, genuinely curious. "Huh - what changed?" The conversation shifts from verdicts to information, Adult-to-Adult, without anyone feeling corrected.
options.lesson: Crossing a Parent-register pastime to Adult - specific, checkable, not a sweeping verdict - is a genuinely different register from the judgmental kind. Same topic, same friendliness, different register.

options.text: Say, "God, this is exactly what my mother used to say about me and TV. Makes me feel about eight years old."
options.outcome: Rosita laughs, surprised into something more personal herself. "Mine too, actually." The pastime drops into shared memory instead of shared verdicts.
options.lesson: Child-register pastiming - going back and replaying old feelings - is just as real a register as Parent or Adult; it's not wrong, it's a third way of playing the same topic.

options.text: Say, with a little edge: "Well, some of us actually monitor what our kids watch."
options.outcome: Rosita's smile tightens. "Well. Must be nice to have the time." The pastime just curdled toward something sharper.
options.lesson: This isn't a pastime reply anymore - it's a dig wrapped in agreement, exactly the kind of opening move that can tip a comfortable pastime into a game if either person picks it up.

beats.line: I don't know, I just feel like I'm failing him somehow - like this is going to be the thing he remembers about his childhood, his dad being distracted all the time.
cues: catastrophic leap ('this is going to be the thing')

options.text: Ask plainly: "What's actually been happening this week - can you give me one example?"
options.outcome: Dev stops fidgeting. "Okay - actually, just Tuesday night, I was on my phone during dinner. That's it, really." One concrete thing, now something he can actually change.
options.lesson: Asking for a specific example crosses a Child-register pastime - global, catastrophic feeling - into Adult, one checkable fact. The same move that works on a Parent-register pastime works here too.

options.text: Reassure him warmly: "No, no, you're a great dad, don't even think that."
options.outcome: Dev nods, comforted for the moment, but the specific worry never actually gets looked at.
options.lesson: Comforting Child with Nurturing Parent feels kind and keeps the pastime warm, but it answers the feeling, not the specific, checkable thing underneath it.

options.text: Match his worry: "Oh, I know, I feel exactly the same, it's the worst, isn't it."
options.outcome: They sit in the shared worry for a minute. It feels bonding, and neither of them is any closer to knowing what, if anything, needs to change.
options.lesson: Matching Child-register worry with your own is comfortable and complementary, but like any pastime it stays in feeling-talk rather than moving toward anything checkable.

options.text: Say, "Honestly, compared to some parents, you're doing fine" - implying some parents aren't.
options.outcome: Dev manages a weak smile, but glances toward Rosita, still mid-rant by the gate. The comparison handed him someone to feel superior to instead of a worry to solve.
options.lesson: A comparison-stroke resolves the bad feeling by creating a target, not by addressing anything - the same discount-shaped move as the earlier dig, just aimed downward instead of sideways.

fields.label: Draw the vectors for Rosita's opening line, and for your best (Adult-crossing) reply.
In under 60 words: name the three registers the 'same' parenting pastime can be played in, and what changes between them.

echo.setting: A week later: the office Slack channel for 'wins'.
echo.shape: same three-register question - is this post Parent, Adult, or Child?
